title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: At the end of the evening Kitty told her mother about her conversation with Levin, and despite all the pity she felt for him, she was glad at the thought that she had received an _offer_. She had no doubt that she had acted rightly. But after she had gone to bed, for a long time she could not sleep. One impression followed her relentlessly. It was Levin's face, his scowling brows and his kind eyes looking out in dark dejection beneath them, as he stood listening to her father and glancing at her and at Vronsky. And she felt so sorry for him that tears came to her eyes. But immediately she thought of the man for whom she had given him up. She vividly recalled his manly, resolute face, his noble self-possession, the good nature that showed in everything he did toward everyone. She remembered the love of the man she loved, and once more all was joy in her soul, and she lay on the pillow smiling with happiness. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry; but what could I do? It's not my fault," she said to herself; but an inner voice told her something else. Whether she felt remorse for having won Levin's love or for having refused him, she could not tell. But her happiness was poisoned by doubts. "Lord, have mercy on us; Lord, have mercy on us; Lord, have mercy on us!" she repeated to herself until she fell asleep.
Meanwhile downstairs, in the prince's little library, one of those scenes that so often took place between the parents about their favorite daughter was unfolding.

"What? I'll tell you what!" the prince shouted, waving his arms and once again wrapping his squirrel-lined dressing-gown around him. "That you've no pride, no dignity; that you're disgracing your daughter, ruining her, with this vulgar, stupid matchmaking!"
"But really, for mercy's sake, prince, what have I done?" said the princess, almost in tears.

She, pleased and happy after the conversation with her daughter, had gone in to the prince to say good-night as usual, and although she had no intention of telling him about Levin's offer and Kitty's refusal, she nonetheless hinted to her husband that she thought things were practically settled with Vronsky and that he would declare himself as soon as his mother arrived. And at those words the prince had at once flown into a rage and begun to use unseemly language.

"What have you done? I'll tell you what. First of all, you're trying to land an eligible gentleman, and all Moscow will be talking about it, and with good reason. If you have evening parties, invite everyone — don't pick out the possible suitors. Invite all the young bucks. Hire a piano player and let them dance, not the way you do things these days, hunting for good matches. It makes me sick, sick to see it, and you've gone on with it until you've turned the poor girl's head. Levin is a thousand times the better man. As for this little Petersburg dandy, they're turned out by the machine, all on one pattern, all precious rubbish. But even if he were a prince of the blood, my daughter need not run after anyone."
"But what have I done?"
"Why, you've..." the prince shouted angrily.
"I know that if one were to listen to you," the princess cut in, "we'd never marry our daughter off. If that's how it's to be, we may as well move to the country."
"Well, and we'd better."
"But wait a minute. Am I trying to chase them down? I'm not trying to chase them down in the least. A young man, and a very nice one, has fallen in love with her, and she, I think..."

"Oh yes, you think! And what if she really is in love and he's no more thinking of marriage than I am! Oh, that I should live to see it! Ah! Spiritualism! Ah! Nice! Ah! The ball!" And the prince, imagining he was mimicking his wife, made a mincing curtsey at each word. "And that's how we're preparing wretchedness for Kitty — and she really has got the notion into her head..."
"But what makes you suppose so?"

"I don't suppose; I know. We have eyes for such things, even if women don't. I can see a man who has serious intentions — that's Levin — and I can see a peacock, like this featherhead, who's only amusing himself."
"Oh, well, once you've got an idea into your head..."
"Well, you'll remember my words, but too late — just as with Dolly."
"All right, all right, we won't talk about it," the princess cut in, remembering her unlucky Dolly.
"By all means, and good-night!"
And making the sign of the cross over each other, husband and wife parted with a kiss, each still holding to his own opinion.

The princess had at first been quite sure that the evening had settled Kitty's future and that there could be no doubt about Vronsky's intentions, but her husband's words had unsettled her. And as she returned to her own room, in dread of the unknown future, she too, like Kitty, repeated several times in her heart, "Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy."
